name: Jamal Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the contractor's yard by half seven, load the van from the cages, and I'm out doing around 140 drops in the estates on the east side by eight. It's an online retailer's parcels, and the app scans every drop and tells the contractor how fast I'm going. I like the walking and I know every short cut, but the stairs in the tower blocks kill my knees by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's in your life outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, renting a one-bed above a barber's on the high road. Sunday I'm at my mum's for dinner with my two sisters, every week, no excuses. My dad was a bus mechanic for 30 years, and he still says I should have done an apprenticeship instead of driving, which, fair enough. I've used one of those AI chat things a couple of times, mostly to sort out a parking fine letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I never thought a computer was going to carry a parcel up eleven floors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to the lads at the yard, the ones who said we'd all be replaced by drones by now. Online I don't really say much. Maybe a laughing face in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change my real problem, which is pay. The contractor cut us from 1.20 a drop to 1.05 in March and called it a route review. That hurts more than any AI ever has, because I'm doing the same stairs for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd finally look at what my dad keeps on about, a gas engineer apprenticeship. Not because of AI, just because the drop rate keeps falling. I'd put 100 a month away from now till next summer so I can afford a year on a lower apprentice wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Normal. Bit tired. Nothing dramatic, just the same squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you call it a squeeze?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent went up 60 in the summer and the drop rate went down, so I'm paying more to earn less. I've got about three months saved. It's fine, but I watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you started the apprenticeship, what would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be made up, and she'd tell the whole street. My mum thinks driving is a job for now and a trade is a job for life. She'd probably offer to have me back home to save rent, and I'd probably say no out of pride.

say: I'd tell the lads at the yard **I told you so** about the drones.
I'd keep quiet online, maybe a **laughing face** in the group chat.
think: The contractor's **drop rate cut** hurts more than any AI has.
Rent up 60 and pay down means paying more to **earn less**.
do: Keep doing my **140 drops** a day on the east side.
Look at a **gas engineer apprenticeship**, like my dad keeps saying.
Save **100 a month** till next summer for an apprentice year.
feel: **Normal and tired**, with the same steady money squeeze.
S0.quote: The contractor cut us from 1.20 a drop to 1.05 in March and called it a route review.
fieldNote: His pressure is the **contractor's pay**, not technology at all.
His dad's push for a **trade** shapes his plans even in a calm scenario.
His **pride** stops him moving back to his mum's to save rent.
Uneasy: work is there but pay is sliding and savings are only three months.

steps.text: Keep doing the east-side parcel drops for the contractor
Look into a gas engineer apprenticeship near home
Put 100 a month aside until next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office stuff gets eaten up, and the robots come in slow. I'm not at a desk, so I'd be watching it from the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the yard I'd say it's the office lot who should worry, not us. To my mates I'd say learn a trade, which is my dad talking through me. I'd keep it down to earth, nothing political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it hits me from the side. The contractor's office already runs on software, and if AI plans the routes even tighter, they'll add 20 drops and say it's the same day. I've seen the robot lockers going up at the supermarket too, so I know where it heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the gas apprenticeship applications this winter, not next summer, because I'd see the office jobs going and people moving into trades. I'd use the AI app to help with the application, since my sister says it's good for that. And I'd ask the contractor for a Saturday route to save a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, because people still need parcels and boilers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said office people would move into trades. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. If every laid-off bank clerk wants a gas apprenticeship, I'm in a queue with people who've got degrees. That's why I'd want to move first, before the queue forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the yard would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mo, who's 50 and been driving 20 years. He can't do the stairs much longer, and he won't learn a new trade at his age. I'd worry about him more than me.

say: I'd say at the yard the **office lot** should worry, not drivers.
I'd tell mates to **learn a trade**, which is really my dad talking.
think: Tighter AI routes would mean **20 more drops** for the same day.
The **robot lockers** at the supermarket show where it's heading.
Laid-off office workers could **crowd the trades** before I get in.
do: Apply for **gas apprenticeships** this winter instead of next summer.
Use the **AI app** to help with the applications.
Ask the contractor for a **Saturday route** to save faster.
feel: A bit uneasy, but **not scared**, because people still need parcels and **boilers**.
S1.quote: If every laid-off bank clerk wants a gas apprenticeship, I'm in a queue with people who've got degrees.
fieldNote: He spots a **second-order risk**: office workers flooding into trades.
He'll use AI **for a job application**, but only once his sister vouches for it.
His concern for **Mo, an older driver**, shows a strong sense of loyalty.
Uneasy: his own hands-on work holds for now, but he's moving early.

steps.text: Apply for gas engineer apprenticeships this winter
Use an AI app to write the apprenticeship applications
Take a Saturday route to save faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? And robots carrying parcels by 2031. That's quick. I'd be 32 and out of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being rushed by people who don't have to live with it. At my mum's on Sunday I'd say we need to look after our own, because nobody else will. I'd probably vote for whoever promised to slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the van is gone by 2031. The thinking part goes first, so the contractor's office empties out in 2028, and then a robot does the stairs three years later. The trade I wanted might not be safe either, because a gas apprenticeship takes four years and I'd finish right as the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the apprenticeship straight away, because fixing an old boiler in a cramped cupboard is the last thing a robot will manage. I'd give up the flat and move back to my mum's, pride or not, to make the apprentice wage work. I'd keep driving weekends for the contractor as long as there's anything left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being shoved. I don't like being rushed, I like to see a thing work before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back to your mum's. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say about time, and my dad would say nothing but he'd clear the box room that night. I'd hate it, I'm 27. But family is what you lean on, not the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the apprenticeship places all filled up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go labouring for a heating firm for nothing much and learn on the job. My uncle knows a fella with a plumbing van. I'd ring him the same week.

say: I'd say it's **being rushed** by people who don't have to live with it.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised to slow it down.
think: The van job is **gone by 2031**, after the contractor's office empties in 2028.
A **four-year apprenticeship** would finish right as the robots come.
do: Give up the flat and **move back** to my mum's to live on an apprentice wage.
Keep **weekend driving** for the contractor while it lasts.
feel: Like being **shoved**, when I'd rather see a thing work before I jump.
S2.quote: Fixing an old boiler in a cramped cupboard is the last thing a robot will manage.
fieldNote: He maps the **2028 and 2031 dates** onto his own job precisely.
Moving home costs him **pride**, but he chooses family over state help.
He has a **fallback** for the fallback: labouring via his uncle's contact.
Alarmed: he expects to lose his job within about five years and must restart on low pay.

steps.text: Start a gas engineer apprenticeship straight away
Give up the flat above the barber's
Move into the box room at his mum and dad's
Vote for whoever promises to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots doing the parcels around 2034. That's a fair bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort yourself out if you get on with it. I'd tell my younger cousin to skip the driving altogether and go straight into a trade. That's the kind of thing I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gives me time to do the apprenticeship properly and finish before the robots arrive. I'd be qualified by about 2030, with four years to build up my own customers. I think I'd still lose the driving income, but I'd have something else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply this winter, start next autumn, and keep the flat if I can manage by driving Saturdays. I'd save 150 a month for tools and a small van of my own, because gas engineers need their own kit. Once the AI stuff is proven, I'd use it for quotes and bookings like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I can see the steps, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI once it's proven. What would prove it to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When my mate Dean, who's a plumber, uses it for his invoices and says it saves him an hour a day. I trust Dean more than an advert. If it works for him, I'll copy him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the year before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably stop driving completely and go full time on boilers. I'd rather be ahead of it than be one of the last ones at the yard waiting for the bad news.

say: I'd say there's **time** to sort yourself out if you get on with it.
I'd tell my younger cousin to **skip driving** and go straight into a trade.
think: I could be a **qualified gas engineer** by about 2030, before the robots.
I'd still **lose the driving income**, but have something else by then.
do: Apply this winter and **start the apprenticeship** next autumn.
Save **150 a month** for tools and a small van.
Drive **Saturdays** to keep the flat while I train.
feel: **Anxious but steady**, because I can see the steps.
S3.quote: I'd rather be ahead of it than be one of the last ones at the yard waiting for the bad news.
fieldNote: He waits for **proof from a friend**, his mate Dean, before trusting AI.
Five years lets him **keep his flat**, so his pride survives this scenario.
His plan has **clear dates**: start next autumn, qualified around 2030.
Anxious: he still expects to lose driving, but feels in control.

steps.text: Start a gas engineer apprenticeship next autumn
Save 150 a month for tools and a small van
Copy his friend Dean's AI invoicing once it's proven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and robots by about 2039. I'd be 40. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off, and anyone who panics now is daft. At the yard we'd joke about the robot getting stuck on the eleventh floor. I'd probably keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the risk is I'd get comfortable and keep driving till 35. Then I'd be starting a trade late, with knees already gone from the stairs. My dad started at 16 and he'd tell me not to waste the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the apprenticeship, but maybe in a couple of years, after saving properly, maybe 6,000 first. I'd keep driving full time till then and try to get a better route with fewer tower blocks. By the 2030s I'd want my own small heating business with a van and a couple of regular landlords.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a nag at the back of my mind, but nothing urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about having a family in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, if I meet the right person. A wife and kids, a house, the normal things. I'd want a trade behind me first, so I'm not asking someone to marry a man whose job a robot is about to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most along the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprenticeships that pay enough to live on at 29, not just for 16-year-olds. And firms that actually take older starters. That's it really.

say: I'd say it's **a long way off** and panicking now is daft.
We'd **joke at the yard** about a robot stuck on the eleventh floor.
think: The risk is I'd **get comfortable** and keep driving till 35.
Starting late means starting a trade with **knees already gone**.
do: Save about **6,000** before starting the apprenticeship.
Ask for a **better route** with fewer tower blocks.
Build my own **small heating business** by the 2030s.
feel: **Calmer**, with a **nag** at the back of my mind.
S4.quote: I'm not asking someone to marry a man whose job a robot is about to take.
fieldNote: His **traditional hopes** for marriage and a house shape his timeline.
He fears his own **complacency** more than the robots.
He wants **paid apprenticeships** for older starters, not handouts.
Anxious rather than uneasy: he still expects driving to end before he's 40.

steps.text: Save about 6,000 before starting the apprenticeship
Train as a gas engineer within two years
Build a small heating business with regular landlords

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be starting a four-year apprenticeship that only finishes as the robots come for the hands-on work. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a proper wage for someone in his late twenties. Not a benefit, a start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my knees, and I'm only half joking. Driving parcels is hard on a body, and the robots might take the job just as some of us can't do it anymore. My dad always said a trade outlasts a body, and he was right.

headlineQuote: My dad always said a trade outlasts a body, and he was right.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old parcel driver** doing 140 drops a day on a city's east-side estates.
He's **single**, rents above a barber's and never misses **Sunday dinner** at his mum's.
His dad, a former bus mechanic, keeps pushing a **trade**, and Jamal mostly agrees.
He uses AI only when someone he trusts **proves it works**.
In every AGI picture he heads for a **gas engineer apprenticeship**, faster with less warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his apprenticeship would finish just as robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** with a living wage for people in their late twenties.
